planting.note: Pot rooted cane sections or offsets in spring once nights stay reliably above 60F, using a rich, humus-heavy mix that never fully dries out between waterings.

directions: Dracaena goldieana is a West African understory species prized for broad, short-stalked leaves banded crosswise in silvery gray-green against a deeper green background, a pattern distinct from the narrow solid-colored foliage of the more familiar corn plant relatives. It naturally grows in deep forest shade and so wants more consistent moisture than drought-tolerant dracaenas, with the top inch of soil kept lightly damp rather than allowed to go bone dry. Propagate by rooting short cane sections in warm, humid conditions, and keep humidity elevated to prevent brown leaf-tip scorch. Its compact, bushy habit and tolerance of dim interior light make it a strong candidate for low-light corners where most variegated dracaenas fade.
sources: Kew Science Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Transplant rooted canes into fresh potting mix in spring, and give the broad gold center stripe bright indirect light to keep it from reverting to plain green.

directions: Victoria is a sport of the common corn plant selected for a wide, buttery gold stripe running down the center of each strap-shaped leaf, bordered by dark green margins — a bolder, more saturated color break than the thinner edge variegation seen on many other fragrans cultivars. Like other corn plants it grows as a slow upright cane that can be cut back and will resprout new heads below the cut, letting growers control height over many years. Let the soil dry out between waterings and avoid cold drafts, since chilling quickly shows up as dull or blotchy leaf color. Strong indirect light preserves the yellow banding best; deep shade causes the stripe to narrow and dull toward green over time.

planting.note: Pot rooted cane cuttings in spring in a dense, well-drained houseplant mix and expect a slower, more upright habit than bushier corn plant cultivars.

directions: Art is grown for its notably narrow, stiffly upright leaves compared to the broader straps of a standard corn plant, each blade edged in a thin pale-yellow to cream margin around a dark green center. The slim foliage gives the whole cane a tighter, more architectural silhouette that suits narrow floor spaces and tight interior corners where a typical broad-leaved dracaena would feel crowded. It shares the family's tolerance for low light and irregular watering, but like other variegated forms it holds its best color under bright, indirect light rather than deep shade. Let the potting mix dry out between waterings and wipe dust from the leaves occasionally to keep them photosynthesizing efficiently.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Dracaena Production Guide

common_name: Janet Craig Compacta Dracaena (Dwarf Janet Craig)

planting.note: Pot divisions or rooted offsets into shallow, wide containers in spring — its dense rosette habit suits dish gardens and terrariums better than tall floor-plant pots.

directions: Janet Craig Compacta is a naturally occurring dwarf sport of the standard Janet Craig dracaena, producing tightly whorled rosettes of short, glossy dark-green leaves on a cane that elongates extremely slowly compared to its parent. Because individual leaves stay just a few inches long and the growth habit is so dense, it is one of the few dracaenas well suited to terrariums, dish gardens, and other spaces too small for a full-size cane plant. It shares the same deep shade tolerance and drought resilience as Janet Craig, doing best when the soil is allowed to dry out between waterings and kept away from cold drafts. Its slow pace means a single rooted section can furnish a small container for years before needing to be divided again.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Dracaena Production Guide
